newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: SACKED NZ MINISTER ACCUSES PM OF BULLYING.
newsitem.headline: SACKED NZ MINISTER ACCUSES PM OF BULLYING.

text.p: Less than a day after pledging his vote to the government, sacked Associate Health Minister Neil Kirton on Wednesday accused New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger of bullying and smear tactics.
Speaking on TV One's breakfast news, Kirton said he thought National wanted to back away from the coalition agreement in a number of areas.
"I want to see all those commitments adhered to. So do my colleagues," he said.
"They're not prepared to engage in any bullying tactics from Mr Bolger. They're not going to be rolled as he may roll his own caucus," Kirton said.

"Our caucus is not going to stand by and watch any shenanigans from Mr Bolger. They're going to stand up and say - no, these are the agreements we made and these are the ones we're going to stick to'."
Kirton did not specify which policies he believed National was trying to back off, the New Zealand Press Association said.
He said Bolger had tried to smear him through "selective leaks up and down the country" in recent weeks.

"My colleagues take a dim view of that. They're not going to tolerate assaults on their members and my caucus colleagues. We're not going to stand around and take that sort of nonsense." Bolger said through a spokeswoman that Kirton's comments were "nonsense" and he had hoped Kirton would have moved on since last week.
She said Bolger's office had not been involved in any leaks to the media about Kirton.
Bolger yesterday said he would be disappointed if Kirton continued to personally attack him after his decision yesterday to remain as part of the New Zealand First caucus.
"It would be rather foolish to just stay in there to be an irritant so I have to assume that he's staying in the New Zealand First caucus to make a constructive contribution."
Kirton had angered the National Party at the weekend by accusing Bolger of being untrustworthy.

He said yesterday he would stay with NZ First despite his sacking by party leader Winston Peters, ostensibly for giving a media interview against orders, after long-running and sometimes bitter tensions within the coalition over management of the health portfolio.
Peters yesterday said he had not asked Kirton to stop speaking out against National.
The coalition government has 61 seats comprising 44 conservative National Party MPs and 17 NZ First MPs in the 120 seat single-chamber parliament.
Bolger has refused to rule out bringing lone United Party MP Peter Dunne into the cabinet to shore up the government's one seat majority.
Kirton on Wednesday said bringing in Dunne would anger NZ First MPs as having nine NZ First ministers was a requirement of the coalition agreement.
"I would be very surprised as my colleagues would that that agreement would be broken ... I'm sure they'd have plenty to say about that."
